title: What common prescription frequency abbreviations mean
text: Prescribers often use Latin-derived abbreviations for how often to take a medicine. OD or 'once daily' means one dose a day. BD, BID or 'twice daily' means two doses a day. TDS, TID or 'three times daily' means three doses a day. QDS or QID means four doses a day. 'q8h' means one dose every 8 hours around the clock, which is stricter than 'three times daily'. HS or 'nocte' means at bedtime. PRN means 'as needed' and is usually paired with a maximum number of doses per day. STAT means immediately, as a single dose. If your prescription label and your understanding differ, the pharmacy label is the instruction to follow, and the pharmacist can confirm it.
source_name: ISMP list of error-prone abbreviations; standard pharmacy practice

title: 'Three times a day' versus 'every 8 hours'
text: 'Three times a day' normally means spreading three doses across your waking hours, for example morning, afternoon and evening, roughly 6 to 8 hours apart. 'Every 8 hours' means an evenly spaced 8-hour gap including overnight, so a dose may need to be taken at night. Some antibiotics work better with even spacing, which is why the wording matters. A prescription that only says 'three times a day' does not specify exact clock times, so MediGraph AI will not invent them; your pharmacist can suggest times that fit your routine and any food requirements.
source_name: Standard pharmacy dispensing practice

title: Completing a prescribed antibiotic course
text: Antibiotic courses are prescribed for a specific duration, such as 5 or 7 days. You should take the course exactly as prescribed and discuss it with the prescriber or pharmacist if you feel better early, develop side effects, or miss several doses. Do not keep leftover antibiotics for future illnesses and do not share them. If a rash, breathing difficulty or facial swelling develops, stop and seek urgent medical help, because that can indicate an allergic reaction.
source_name: CDC antibiotic use guidance

title: General guidance on a missed dose
text: General guidance for most medicines is to take a missed dose as soon as you remember, unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case you skip the missed one. Do not take two doses together to catch up unless the leaflet or your pharmacist explicitly says so. Some medicines, including anticoagulants, insulin, contraceptives, anti-epileptics and HIV medicines, have specific missed-dose rules that differ from this general advice, so check the patient information leaflet or ask a pharmacist for those.
source_name: MedlinePlus patient medicine guidance

title: Taking medicines with or without food
text: 'With food' usually means during or just after a meal, which can reduce stomach irritation (common advice for NSAIDs and steroids). 'On an empty stomach' usually means at least 30 to 60 minutes before a meal or two hours after, because food lowers absorption (common for levothyroxine and some antibiotics). Only follow a food instruction that is actually written on your prescription or pharmacy label; if nothing is specified, the pharmacist can tell you what the product leaflet recommends.
source_name: MedlinePlus patient medicine guidance

title: What a drug-drug interaction means
text: A drug-drug interaction happens when one medicine changes how another behaves. Pharmacokinetic interactions change how much drug is in the body: one medicine may block or speed up the liver enzymes (such as CYP3A4 or CYP2C9) or transporters that clear another, raising or lowering its levels. Pharmacodynamic interactions happen when two medicines push the body in the same direction, for example two medicines that both thin the blood, both raise potassium or both cause drowsiness. A flagged interaction does not always mean the combination is forbidden: many are prescribed deliberately with monitoring. What matters is that a clinician knows about the combination.
source_name: FDA guidance on drug interaction labelling

title: How interaction severity categories should be read
text: MediGraph AI groups findings as High concern, Moderate concern, Information available, or No known interaction found in the checked sources. High concern means published labelling describes a serious or contraindicated combination. Moderate concern means a real interaction that is usually managed with monitoring, dose changes or timing changes. Information available means there is something worth knowing, such as a timing or absorption issue. 'No known interaction found in the checked sources' means only that nothing matched in the datasets this tool checked. It is not a statement that the combination is safe: datasets are incomplete, they rarely cover supplements, herbal products or combinations of three or more medicines, and they do not know your kidney function, liver function or genetics.
source_name: MediGraph AI methodology; FDA drug interaction labelling guidance

title: Warning signs of bleeding on blood thinners
text: People taking anticoagulants or antiplatelet medicines should know the warning signs of bleeding: black or tarry stools, blood in the urine, vomiting material that looks like coffee grounds, coughing up blood, unusually heavy or prolonged bleeding from small cuts, large unexplained bruises, nosebleeds that will not stop, and a severe or sudden headache. A severe headache, weakness on one side or confusion can indicate bleeding in the brain and needs emergency care immediately.
source_name: FDA label for warfarin sodium (Warnings); patient counselling information

title: Serotonin syndrome warning signs
text: Serotonin syndrome can occur when medicines that raise serotonin are combined, for example an SSRI antidepressant with tramadol, triptans, linezolid or St John's wort. Early signs are agitation, restlessness, sweating, shivering, fast heartbeat, dilated pupils, diarrhoea and tremor. More severe signs are muscle rigidity or twitching, high fever and confusion. It can develop within hours of a dose change. Severe symptoms are a medical emergency; milder new symptoms should be reported to the prescriber the same day.
source_name: FDA label for tramadol hydrochloride (Warnings)

title: High potassium: why some combinations are monitored
text: Several common medicines raise blood potassium: ACE inhibitors (such as lisinopril and enalapril), ARBs (such as losartan), potassium-sparing diuretics (such as spironolactone) and potassium supplements. Combining them can cause hyperkalaemia, which may produce muscle weakness, tingling, nausea, or an abnormal heart rhythm, sometimes with no symptoms until it is severe. This is why clinicians order potassium and kidney blood tests after starting or increasing these medicines, and why potassium supplements and salt substitutes should only be used when prescribed.
source_name: FDA label for spironolactone (Warnings)

title: Statins and muscle symptoms
text: Statins can cause muscle aches, and rarely serious muscle injury (myopathy or rhabdomyolysis). The risk rises when a statin is combined with medicines that raise its blood level, such as clarithromycin, certain antifungals, or verapamil, which is why simvastatin is often paused during a clarithromycin course. Report new, unexplained muscle pain, tenderness or weakness, especially with dark urine or fever, to a clinician promptly.
source_name: FDA label for simvastatin (Warnings and Contraindications)

title: What NSAIDs are and their main risks
text: NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) such as ibuprofen, naproxen and diclofenac reduce pain, fever and inflammation by inhibiting COX enzymes. Their main risks are stomach and intestinal ulcers or bleeding, reduced kidney function, fluid retention and raised blood pressure, and an increased risk of heart attack and stroke with long-term higher-dose use. These risks are higher in older adults, in people with kidney disease, heart failure or ulcer history, and when combined with anticoagulants, steroids or SSRIs. Taking two NSAIDs at once adds risk without adding benefit, and aspirin counts as an NSAID for that purpose.
source_name: FDA NSAID class labelling and Drug Safety Communication

title: Why opioids plus benzodiazepines carry a boxed warning
text: The FDA requires a boxed warning on opioids and benzodiazepines about combining them. Both depress the central nervous system, so together they can cause profound sedation, dangerously slow or shallow breathing, coma and death. The risk is highest when either medicine is started or its dose increased, and when alcohol is also involved. If both are genuinely needed, they are prescribed at the lowest effective doses with close follow-up. Seek emergency help for very slow breathing, bluish lips, or someone who cannot be woken.
source_name: FDA Drug Safety Communication on opioid and benzodiazepine combination

title: Drug allergy versus side effect
text: A true drug allergy is an immune reaction: hives, widespread rash, swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, wheeze, or anaphylaxis with collapse. A side effect or intolerance is a predictable pharmacological effect, such as nausea from an antibiotic, drowsiness from an antihistamine, or itching from morphine. The difference matters because a recorded 'allergy' that was really a side effect can block useful medicines for life, while a genuine allergy must be avoided across the whole drug class. Only a clinician can reclassify a recorded allergy, so keep it on your record and discuss it rather than disregarding it.
source_name: FDA labelling guidance on hypersensitivity reactions; standard allergy practice

title: Penicillin allergy and related antibiotics
text: A documented penicillin allergy means other penicillins, including amoxicillin, amoxicillin/clavulanate and ampicillin, should be avoided unless an allergy specialist has reassessed it. Cross-reactivity with cephalosporins exists but is much lower than the figures once quoted, and many people labelled penicillin-allergic in childhood are not truly allergic when formally tested. Deciding this requires a clinician; never take a penicillin-class antibiotic yourself to test a recorded allergy.
source_name: FDA penicillin class labelling (Contraindications)

title: What RxNorm is and why names are normalised
text: RxNorm is a drug terminology produced by the US National Library of Medicine. It gives each clinical drug concept a stable identifier called an RXCUI and links brand names to their generic ingredients, so 'Tylenol', 'paracetamol' and 'acetaminophen' resolve to the same ingredient. MediGraph AI normalises every medication name it extracts before checking interactions, because interaction datasets are keyed on ingredients rather than brands. Normalising also catches duplicate therapy, such as a branded cold remedy that already contains the paracetamol you are taking separately.
source_name: National Library of Medicine, RxNorm

title: What openFDA drug labels provide
text: openFDA publishes structured product labelling for medicines approved in the United States, including the indications, dosage, warnings, contraindications and drug-interaction sections written by the manufacturer and reviewed by the FDA. It is a good source for what a label formally says about a medicine, but it reflects US labelling, it is not personalised to you, and label text can differ between countries and between brands of the same generic. Your own patient information leaflet and your pharmacist remain the authority for the product you actually hold.
source_name: openFDA drug label API

title: What to confirm with your pharmacist
text: Useful things to confirm with a pharmacist when you collect a prescription: what each medicine is for; the exact times to take it and whether that is with or without food; what to do about a missed dose; which side effects are expected and which need urgent attention; how long the course lasts and whether a review is needed; whether it interacts with anything else you take, including over-the-counter painkillers, supplements and herbal products; whether alcohol matters; and how to store it. Bring a full list of everything you take, including things you buy yourself, because those are the items most often missing from clinical records.
source_name: MedlinePlus: Taking medicines safely

title: Medication reactions that need emergency care
text: Call emergency services immediately for: difficulty breathing or wheeze that starts after a dose; swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat; a rash that spreads quickly, blisters, or peels, especially with fever or mouth sores; fainting, collapse or confusion; chest pain; a seizure; severe or sudden headache or one-sided weakness while on a blood thinner; vomiting blood or passing black tarry stools; or very slow, shallow breathing and unresponsiveness after an opioid or sedative. Do not wait for a routine appointment for any of these, and take your medication list with you.
source_name: FDA MedWatch safety information; standard emergency guidance

title: Duplicate therapy and hidden ingredients
text: Duplicate therapy means taking two products that contain the same ingredient or two medicines from the same class. It is a common cause of accidental overdose, because combination cold, flu and pain products often contain paracetamol (acetaminophen), ibuprofen, an antihistamine or a decongestant without that being obvious from the brand name. Check the active ingredients panel of anything you buy yourself, and show the pharmacist your full list before adding an over-the-counter product.
source_name: FDA Drug Safety Communication on acetaminophen-containing products

title: Grapefruit, alcohol and other non-drug interactions
text: Interactions are not limited to prescription medicines. Grapefruit juice inhibits intestinal CYP3A4 and can raise levels of some statins, calcium channel blockers and other medicines. Alcohol adds to the sedation of opioids, benzodiazepines and antihistamines, and adds liver risk with paracetamol. St John's wort is a strong enzyme inducer that can make anticoagulants, contraceptives and many other medicines less effective. Calcium, iron, magnesium and antacids can bind some antibiotics and levothyroxine and reduce their absorption. Tell your prescriber about supplements and herbal products: they are frequently missing from interaction databases, including this tool's.
source_name: FDA consumer update on grapefruit and medicines

title: How the MediGraph knowledge graph is used
text: MediGraph AI builds a graph in which each Patient, Medication, Prescription, Condition, Allergy and Interaction is a node. Edges record PATIENT_TAKES, PRESCRIBED_IN, PATIENT_ALLERGIC_TO, PATIENT_HAS_CONDITION, INTERACTS_WITH and CONTRAINDICATED_WITH relationships. Representing the data this way makes safety questions into path queries: an allergy warning is a short path from a Patient to an Allergy class that also reaches a prescribed Medication, and an interaction is an INTERACTS_WITH edge between two medications the same patient takes. The graph runs on Neo4j when configured, and on an in-process NetworkX graph otherwise; the findings are identical because both are built from the same records.
source_name: MediGraph AI architecture documentation

title: How the chatbot finds its answers
text: The chatbot uses retrieval-augmented generation. Your question is first matched against a local corpus containing this reference library, the medication records for your prescriptions, and the findings of your own safety report. The best-matching passages are retrieved, and the answer is composed only from those passages, with the source of each passage shown. When no passage is relevant enough, the chatbot says that it does not have reliable information rather than guessing. It is restricted to explaining what your prescription and the retrieved sources already say: it does not diagnose conditions, recommend new medicines, or set doses.
source_name: MediGraph AI architecture documentation

title: Limits of automated prescription parsing
text: Automated extraction of medication name, strength, dose, frequency, duration and route is reliable for clearly written text but imperfect. Abbreviations are ambiguous, handwriting and OCR introduce errors, look-alike medicine names exist, and tapering or 'as directed' instructions do not fit a simple structure. MediGraph AI marks any field it could not find as needing verification rather than filling in a plausible value, because an invented dose or duration is more dangerous than a blank one. Always check the parsed table against the written prescription or pharmacy label before relying on it.
source_name: MediGraph AI methodology; ISMP guidance on prescription abbreviations

title: Storing and disposing of medicines
text: Most medicines keep best in a cool, dry place out of direct sunlight and out of reach of children; bathrooms are usually too humid. Some products, including many insulins and liquid antibiotics, need refrigeration and have a short life after opening, which the label states. Do not use medicines past their expiry date or ones that have changed colour or smell. Return unused or expired medicines to a pharmacy take-back scheme rather than flushing them, unless the leaflet specifically instructs otherwise.
source_name: FDA guidance on safe medicine disposal

title: What MediGraph AI can and cannot do
text: MediGraph AI reads prescription text you enter, structures it, normalises medication names, checks them against a curated interaction dataset and your recorded allergies and conditions, and explains what it found with sources. It cannot diagnose a condition, decide whether a medicine is right for you, set or change a dose, tell you to stop or start anything, or account for information it has not been given, such as your blood test results, kidney function, pregnancy status if unrecorded, or other medicines you did not enter. Its dataset is a curated subset rather than a complete clinical interaction database, so an empty result is not a safety guarantee. Use it to arrive at your pharmacist or prescriber with better questions, not to replace their judgement.
source_name: MediGraph AI product documentation
